title: Checking data with zod

story: Before Nova claims a machine for RH-1234, a cheap model call reads the ticket and answers one question: is it ready, should Nova ask the requester first, or should the ticket go back to them? The answer comes back as JSON, and our code branches on its verdict field. TypeScript is sure the verdict is "ready", "ask" or "hand_back", because the code says JSON.parse(text) as Readiness.

One morning the model writes "Ready" with a capital R. Nothing crashes. The code compares, finds neither "ready" nor "ask", falls into the last branch, and hands a small, perfectly clear ticket back to Sean with a polite note. TypeScript saw nothing wrong, because by the time the code runs, the types are gone.
hook.question: How do I check data that comes from outside my program, such as a request body, a file or a model's answer, so that a wrong shape is caught at the door, and how do I avoid writing the same shape twice?

p: TypeScript types exist only while tsc checks your code. Lesson p1-1 showed that tsx removes them and runs what is left, and the same happens in the build: the JavaScript that Node runs has no types at all. So JSON.parse returns any, and writing as Readiness does not check anything. It is a promise you make to the compiler, and the compiler believes you.

Inside your own program that is usually fine, because tsc checked every place that builds the value. It is not fine at the edge of the program, where data arrives from somewhere tsc never saw: an HTTP body, a YAML file, an environment variable, and above all a model's answer. Every one of those needs a real check that runs, and that is what a schema is for.

read.h: One schema, and the type comes with it
p: zod is a small library for describing the shape of data with code that runs. z.object lists the fields, z.enum allows exactly a few strings, z.string().min(1) refuses an empty string, and z.array(...).max(5) refuses a sixth question. The rules live right on the fields.

The part that saves you from writing the shape twice is z.infer. It reads the schema and produces the TypeScript type, so Readiness the type and Readiness the schema can never disagree: change the schema and the type changes with it. In the platform every shape that crosses a boundary lives in the shared package as a schema, with the type inferred from it under the same name.

notes.text: Exactly one of these three strings. The inferred type is "ready" | "ask" | "hand_back".
A list of strings, five at most.
The type, read from the schema. Using the same name for the value and the type is allowed in TypeScript.

read.h: parse and safeParse at the edge
p: A schema checks data in one of two ways. Readiness.parse(data) returns the data, now with its type, or throws a ZodError. Readiness.safeParse(data) never throws: it returns { success: true, data } or { success: false, error }. z.prettifyError turns the error into lines a person can read, each with the path of the field that is wrong.

Which one to use depends on whose mistake bad data is. At an HTTP route, bad data is the caller's mistake and quite normal, so use safeParse and answer 400 with the problems. For a model's answer inside a Temporal activity, parse is fine: the throw fails the activity, and Temporal retries it, which usually gets a well-formed answer the second time.

notes.text: Never throws. The result says whether the data matched.
Inside this branch result.data has the type Readiness, checked for real.

read.see:
$ npx tsx check.ts
✖ Invalid option: expected one of "ready"|"ask"|"hand_back"
  → at verdict

read.h: The same schema tells the model what to write
p: A model can be asked to answer in a fixed shape. The Claude Agent SDK takes an outputFormat with a JSON Schema, a standard way to describe JSON that many tools understand, and hands back the model's answer as structured_output. You do not write that JSON Schema by hand: z.toJSONSchema(Readiness) writes it from the same zod schema, enum, minLength, maxItems and all.

Then you parse the answer again with the same schema. Asking for a shape is not the same as checking it: JSON Schema cannot say everything zod can, and a model can still answer off-shape. So one schema does three jobs: it gives the TypeScript type, it tells the model what to write, and it checks what came back.

deeper.h: Go deeper: a schema has an input side and an output side
p: A field with .default("low") may be missing in the data you parse, but it is always present in the result. So a schema really has two types: z.input<typeof Plan> is what may come in, and z.infer<typeof Plan> is what parsing gives back. z.toJSONSchema(Plan) describes the output side by default, where the field is required. A model writes the input side, so the planner asks for z.toJSONSchema(Plan, { io: "input" }), where the field may be left out.

For rules that involve several fields, such as "a plan that touches the frontend must describe its screen states", zod has superRefine: a function that looks at the whole object and adds its own issues. The planner sends those issues back to the model to fix.

lab.title: Catch a capital R before it hands back a good ticket
needs: About 10 MB of disk for zod
lab.goal: See an unchecked model answer take the wrong branch, catch it with a zod schema, and turn the same schema into the JSON Schema a model would receive.

guess.q: trust.ts reads { "verdict": "Ready", ... } with JSON.parse(text) as Readiness, where the type says the verdict is "ready" | "ask" | "hand_back". What does it print?

options.text: claim a VM and start planning
options.why: "Ready" and "ready" are different strings, so the first comparison is false.

options.text: A TypeError, because "Ready" is not one of the allowed values
options.why: The allowed values exist only in the type, and the type is gone when the code runs. Nothing compares the value with them.

options.text: hand the ticket back to the requester
options.why: Neither comparison matches, so the code falls into the last branch. The as checked nothing, so the wrong value went straight through.

check.q: A route does const body = JSON.parse(text) as RunScope. A caller sends a scope with repo "evil/fcp". What stops it?

options.text: TypeScript, because RunScope says repo must be a RhinoHealth repo
options.why: A type cannot express "starts with RhinoHealth/", and even if it could, it is gone when the code runs.

options.text: Nothing; the as only silences the compiler, so the bad scope is accepted
options.why: That is why data from outside is checked with RunScope.safeParse, which runs the regex for real and lets the route answer 400.

options.text: JSON.parse, because it checks the object against the type
options.why: JSON.parse knows nothing about your types. It returns any.

check.q: Why do we write the zod schema and use z.infer, instead of writing an interface and a schema side by side?

options.text: Because z.infer makes the code faster
options.why: z.infer exists only for tsc; it produces a type and no code at all.

options.text: Because interfaces are not allowed in ES modules
options.why: Interfaces work fine in ES modules. The problem is keeping two descriptions of one shape the same.

options.text: Because two separate descriptions of one shape drift apart, and an inferred type cannot
options.why: Change the schema and the type changes with it, so the check and the type always describe the same data.

check.q: The readiness check asks the model for output in the shape of z.toJSONSchema(Readiness). Why does it still call Readiness.parse on the answer?

options.text: Because asking for a shape is not checking it: the model can still answer off-shape, and JSON Schema cannot express every zod rule
options.why: The schema is both the request and the check. A bad answer throws, and Temporal retries the activity.

options.text: Because structured_output is a string that must be parsed as JSON first
options.why: structured_output is already an object. parse here is about checking the shape, not reading text.

options.text: It does not need to; the SDK guarantees the shape
options.why: Treat the model's answer like any other data from outside your program: check it at the door.

p: Every shape that crosses a boundary in the platform is a zod schema in the shared package (shared/src/schemas.ts), with its type inferred under the same name: the run scope the orchestrator sends to the broker, the readiness verdict, the plan, a routine's charter. The broker safeParses every scope before it touches the database.

The readiness check runs Sonnet 5.5 at low effort with no tools and an outputFormat built by z.toJSONSchema(Readiness), then parses the answer again. The planner asks for z.toJSONSchema(Plan, { io: "input" }), runs Plan.safeParse on the result, and sends any problems back to the planner session to fix, including superRefine rules such as "a plan that changes the frontend must describe its screen states".

tickets.why: The readiness check: a zod schema, z.toJSONSchema for the model, and Readiness.parse on the answer.
The Plan schema in the shared package, io: "input" for the model, safeParse errors sent back to the planner, and superRefine rules.
The broker checks every run scope against its schema before it stores it.

words.plain: A description of a data shape written as code that runs, so it can check real data.
Reads a zod schema and gives the matching TypeScript type, so the two can never drift apart.
parse returns the checked data or throws; safeParse never throws and returns success or the problems.
A standard format for describing JSON. Models and many tools read it; z.toJSONSchema writes it for you.
A model answer in a fixed JSON shape that you asked for with a JSON Schema.

review.q: From memory: write a zod schema for a verdict that is ready, ask or hand_back, with a non-empty reason, and the line that gives its type.
review.a: const Readiness = z.object({ verdict: z.enum(["ready", "ask", "hand_back"]), reason: z.string().min(1) }); type Readiness = z.infer<typeof Readiness>;

review.q: List four places where data enters a platform service from outside and needs a schema.
review.a: HTTP request bodies (like the broker's run scope), files we load (YAML charters, settings), environment variables, and model answers (readiness verdicts, plans). Anything tsc did not see being built.

remember: Types vanish when the code runs, so check outside data with a zod schema at the door, infer the type from it, and hand the same schema to the model.
